notes.claim: Regulation 641.1 requires every installation, during erection and on completion, to be inspected and tested before being put into service.

Zs measured at ambient temperature must be allowed for the rise in conductor resistance under load before comparing with the maximum values; Megger describes an 80% rule, and a forum contributor says calculated R1+R2 should be for 70 degrees C.
To verify disconnection in 0.4 s on a TN system, the measured earth fault loop impedance must not exceed the corrected maximum, as the NICEIC example sets out for a 6 A type B breaker.

The Electrical Installation Certificate is valid only with the schedule of inspections and schedule(s) of test results, and the designer's recommended interval to the first periodic inspection must be entered.

The interval should reflect the frequency and quality of maintenance the installation can expect, agreed between designer, installer and others; for later reports Regulation 653.4 requires an explanation.
The assignment asks the designer to specify the maximum period to the first periodic inspection (9a) and to state the documents given to the client at handover (9b).

Dan's On-Site Guide prints maximum measured Zs values for a test at 10 °C (Appendix B): the Table 41.3 design values divided by 1.25, because BS 7671's figures are for conductors at their maximum operating temperature. For another test temperature Table B8 multiplies by (ambient + 230) ÷ (10 + 230); the guide's example is 25 °C, 32 A type B: 1.1 × 1.06 = 1.179 Ω.

Table B6 of the guide prints, at 10 °C, 2.91 Ω for a 6 A type C and 1.75 Ω for a 10 A type C (page image checked): the case file's 3.64 Ω and 2.19 Ω divided by 1.25. The lesson quotes only these two values, never the table.

The 0.8 factor of BS 7671 Appendix 3 allows for the rise in conductor resistance between a cold test and a loaded cable (IET wording). Appendix 3 calls it one method and does not rule out others; the OSG and GN3 tables already include it. An IET contributor calls 80% a somewhat arbitrary rule of thumb about test against operating temperature, not heating in the fault. Taught as one accepted method; the OSG's 1.25 divisor is the same idea.

A cold reading compared directly with the Chapter 41 table figure can pass a circuit that would fail when warm; those tables assume conductors at full operating temperature, so a cold reading should not exceed 80% of the tabulated value (trade summary of Appendix 3).

For verification the designer gives the line and cpc resistances at the ambient temperature expected during the tests (OSG). Table I1 values are at a 20 °C reference, which Table I2 moves to the test ambient; this is a different step from the Table I3 multiplier up to operating temperature, which Dan's slides describe as correcting 'as if the circuit were operating'.

Zs at the end of a circuit can be measured directly, or found as Ze measured at the origin plus measured (R1+R2), or as the distributor's declared Ze plus measured (R1+R2). A direct reading is usually less than Ze + (R1+R2) because of parallel earth return paths through bonded parts, so it is allowed for when comparing with design data, and Zs is never worked backwards to find R1+R2.

Why installed readings usually come in lower than the design: the test is at ambient not operating temperature; a direct Zs reading includes parallel paths that the Ze test leaves out; and the design uses declared maximum Ze, maximum tabulated resistances and, for the showroom, lengths scaled off 1:50 drawings with no printed dimensions. The last two are the course's own reading, not a source's statement, and the lesson says so.

The inspector compares each circuit's Zs with the maximum for its device and cable (OSG Appendix B), and the model schedule of test results has a column for the maximum permitted Zs; where it comes from a source other than the Chapter 41 tables, the source is stated in the remarks.
Verification of voltage drop is not normally required during initial verification (OSG), where it is wanted it is typically evaluated from the measured circuit impedances.

The inspector checks against the design: the inspection checklist includes conductors selected for current-carrying capacity and voltage drop in accordance with the design, and the presence of diagrams, instructions and similar information. Inspection and testing happen during erection and on completion, before service; the certificate with its schedules goes to the person ordering the work.

What a designer gives the inspector (C&G P2 Q8a shape): a diagram, chart or schedule (points, cable size and type per circuit, the protection against shock, the devices and isolation, anything vulnerable to a test); the supply characteristics, by enquiry or measurement; the maximum permitted Zs per circuit and its source; the expected R1+R2 at test ambient. The text of Regulation 611.2 was not found in a quotable source, so the lesson does not attribute the list to it.

The first periodic inspection interval is the designer's recommendation and is entered on the certificate; it takes into account the frequency and quality of maintenance the installation can reasonably be expected to receive, and is agreed between designer, installer and other relevant parties (Dan's OSG Appendix G, p.189).

Industry guidance is IET Guidance Note 3 Table 3.2, quoted by an insurer and a trade page: commercial 5 years; offices, shops, laboratories 5; industrial 3. GN3 is not in Dan's materials and no row names a car showroom, so the lesson takes commercial (5 years), says so, and notes that the IET calls these recommendations, with engineering judgement and Regulation 652.1's factors deciding. Cars driven over the floor (pack p.3) are a reason to shorten it.

Handover documents: the Electrical Installation Certificate with its schedules (valid only with them), circuit charts or diagrams, the notices, and where the specification calls for them an O&M manual and building logbook; a copy of the certificate with schedules goes in the CDM project health and safety documentation; Dan's EAL checklist 4.3 looks for an O&M manual with the related drawings. Whether an O&M manual is a legal duty is argued, so it is taught as what the specification and contract require.

For a building other than a dwelling, Approved Document L volume 2 requires a commissioning notice to the building control body and owner for fixed building services that need commissioning, and says the building log book may refer to the O&M manuals or the health and safety file. Whether the showroom's lighting controls need it is for building control, and the lesson says so.

Which appendix holds the temperature comparison differs between Dan's sources: the City & Guilds papers (2016, 2017, 17th Edition era) say Appendix 14; a trade summary says it is Appendix 3 in the current book (Appendix 14 in the 17th Edition); IET staff point to Appendix 3 of the 2018+A2 book. The lesson names the rule, tells Dan to find it in his own copy, and gives no page.
